assessmentSummary.identity: Mini-Band Lateral Walk is a repeated resisted lateral travel cycle. With an intact continuous loop band above both knees, use a shallow athletic stance, take a controlled lateral lead step, follow with the trailing foot without losing specified band tension, continue the declared count, then reverse direction. It is not no-band side stepping, ankle/foot-band walking, diagonal or forward monster walking, lateral lunging, squatting, clamshell work, testing, or fatigue-to-failure work.
currentCardFindings: Source 68 supplies a broad band-walk label but not a precise placement, cycle, count rule, fatigue boundary, alternate graph, calibration, or review contract.
Legacy coaching material describes above-knee, ankle, and foot band placements together; placement materially changes the resistance lever and must be explicit.
Three legacy URLs exist only as unverified human-review candidates.

proposedTaxonomy.laterality: bilateral repeated travel with direction reversal
proposedTaxonomy.intent: low-dose elastic-resistance lateral travel and movement observation

proposedDosage.progressWhen: the exact specified cycle remains controlled in both directions without symptoms or downstream-quality cost

coachCues: Inspect the loop and set it above both knees
Use a short clear lane and a shallow stance
Lead sideways, then follow without snapping the feet together
Watch band tension, pelvis, knees, feet, and both-direction count
athleteInstructions: Set the band above your knees and take small quiet side steps
Lead, then follow while keeping the band gently tensioned
Reverse only after the declared count
Stop for pain, loss of balance, or a band problem

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Materialize the above-knee loop-band lateral walk as a candidate-only exact definition. Treat step width, cadence, and selected tension as modifiers within it; make ankle and foot placements explicit variants; keep no-band, diagonal/forward, lunge, squat, clamshell, and test tasks separate.

currentCardSnapshot.description: With an intact continuous loop band above both knees, take controlled repeated lateral lead steps and trailing-foot follows on a clear level surface while maintaining the declared band tension and stance. Complete the declared count in one direction, then reverse. This excludes no-band side stepping, ankle or foot band placements, diagonal or forward monster walks, lateral lunges, squats, clamshells, testing, and fatigue-to-failure work.

environment.surface: clear level non-slip lateral travel lane
environment.space: room to take declared lateral steps and reverse without collision
environment.changeRule: Changing band placement, tension, direction, step path, stance, surface, dose, tempo, or intent requires revalidation.

can manage the assigned loop band and stop signal
can retain the declared above-knee placement and controlled step-follow cycle without symptom escalation
excludeOrEscalate: symptom, restriction, band, surface, balance, communication, or logistics conflict
sharp, increasing, unfamiliar, neurologic, circulation, breathing, dizziness, balance, or other stop concern

evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Mini-Band Lateral Walk is a repeated lateral lead-step and trailing-foot follow on a level clear surface while a continuous loop band remains above both knees. Each direction is completed before reversing.
The source supports elastic-resistance context but does not establish a universal Mini-Band Lateral Walk form, band placement, dose, or outcome; those are candidate contracts requiring review.

claims: The adjacent lateral-lunge source informs frontal-plane task observation only and does not validate the band-walk load or exact technique. Record step width, toe direction, trunk/pelvis motion, knee path, band tension, and trailing-foot return.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Difficulty describes only exact task complexity and physical demand, never participant skill, age, proficiency, gender, or classification. The baseline has modest external resistance but requires controlled lateral travel, repeated stance organisation, band handling, and bilateral direction changes.

evidence.sourceTitle: Elastic Resistance Effectiveness on Increasing Strength of Shoulders and Hips
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Elastic resistance, placement, band tension, step count, range, cadence, and downstream session work can change demand. Track steps per direction, band location/tension, stance depth, compensation, symptoms, and downstream lateral or jumping work; no universal recovery interval is claimed.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Use an intact appropriate loop band, clear level non-slip travel lane, adequate lateral clearance, footwear or bare-foot policy appropriate to the facility, a way to stop/exit, and communication. Selection is based on exact task and workout inputs, not a card-level population label.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: No universal step count, band tension, band placement, rest, preparation effect, or readiness threshold is established. Use a conservative quality-limited candidate dose, not a fatigue burn set, and stop before symptoms or uncorrectable loss of the specified cycle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Elastic Resistance Effectiveness on Increasing Strength of Shoulders and Hips
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
claims: Instructions must name the above-knee loop band, athletic stance, small lateral lead step, controlled trailing-foot follow, maintained tension, direction change, and reset. Do not infer a required squat depth, toe angle, step width, or band color.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Appropriate instruction, supervision, environment, progressive exposure, and equipment inspection are safeguards. Stop for pain, new neurologic/circulation/breathing/dizziness symptoms, band failure, unsafe surface, loss of balance, or uncorrectable quality loss.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Use Mini-Band Lateral Walk only when the exact low-dose resisted lateral travel task fits objectives, logistics, fatigue, impact, and downstream demands; it does not promise glute activation, knee stability, treatment, or injury prevention. Any change to band placement/tension, stance, step path, surface, dose, tempo, or substitution reruns validation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Athlete support should show the band location, safe set-up, lead-step/follow sequence, self-check, direction change, and stop prompt in plain language. Exact media match, captions, quality, accessibility, and safety remain unverified until human review.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Coach support should include loop-band integrity and fit, clear lane, precise placement, front/side observation of trunk/pelvis/knee/foot motion, step count in both directions, first quality loss, and escalation for unresolved symptoms. Do not diagnose a glute or knee deficit.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Candidate accessibility supports include a shorter lane, smaller steps, lighter reviewed loop band, stable nearby hand support when revalidated, still sequence, captions, transcript, audio description, and reviewed substitute. They do not prove individual readiness or preserve identity when band resistance is removed.

alternateAssessments.name: Mini-Band Lateral Walk with Smaller Steps
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared shorter lateral step preserves the same above-knee loop-band lead-step/follow cycle.

alternateAssessments.name: Mini-Band Lateral Walk with Slower Cadence
alternateAssessments.rationale: A declared slower cadence preserves the same load placement and lateral cycle.

alternateAssessments.name: Mini-Band Lateral Walk with Band at Ankles
alternateAssessments.rationale: Moving the loop band to the ankles changes the resistance lever while retaining the declared lateral lead-step/follow action.

alternateAssessments.name: Mini-Band Lateral Walk with Band at Feet
alternateAssessments.rationale: Moving the loop band to the feet changes the resistance lever, foot constraint, and load demand while retaining lateral travel.

alternateAssessments.name: No-Band Lateral Step
alternateAssessments.rationale: Removing the required elastic resistance changes the external load method and task definition.

alternateAssessments.name: Monster Walk
alternateAssessments.rationale: Forward, backward, or diagonal travel changes the movement direction and action contract.

alternateAssessments.name: Lateral Lunge
alternateAssessments.rationale: A loaded lateral lunge changes range, vertical loading, and repetition boundary.

alternateAssessments.name: Clamshell
alternateAssessments.rationale: A side-lying open-chain hip action changes base, support, and movement path.
